description: We are representing LOGICA, the Latinx Organization for Growth in Computing and Academics!
summary: Into The Unknown turns NASA SPHEREx infrared observations of any patch of sky into a short "flipbook", so anyone can check whether something moved or changed brightness. This is the blink method Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto. Enter a sky position or pick one of 47 prepared fields. The app aligns the SPHEREx survey passes onto one grid and plays them with a shared brightness stretch, so the comparisons are fair. It offers Blink and Difference modes, ESA Gaia DR3 "should be here" markers and motion arrows, and a click-a-pixel spectrum and light curve. SPHEREx data is public but arrives as multi-extension FITS files reached through Python. We made it a no-login web page for citizen scientists, students and teachers, plus a guided Learn page in English, Spanish and Hindi. Barnard's Star and epsilon Indi B pass our astrometry checks against independent Gaia predictions: the motion error is 0.041 px and 0.031 px, against a 0.2 px limit. We claim no discovery. The tool makes searching for movers like a "Planet X" accessible to everyone.
details:
What it does: Into The Unknown is a free web app with no login. Give it a position on the sky (RA/Dec, an object name, or one of 47 prepared fields, including five challenge targets). It shows the SPHEREx time series of that patch as a flipbook. You can Play all passes, Blink between two, view the Difference from a reference pass (a moving star shows up as a dark/bright pair), or Investigate a pixel to see its spectrum and light curve. ESA Gaia DR3 positions are moved forward to each pass, using proper motion and parallax, and drawn as markers and motion arrows. Every view is a shareable URL. A guided Learn page offers three activities built on real saved data (Barnard's Star motion, RW Aurigae wavelength comparison, WISE 0855 uncertainty) in English, Spanish and Hindi, with shareable PNG postcards.

How it works: The React + TypeScript frontend talks only to our Python FastAPI backend. The backend finds SPHEREx Level 2 exposures through NASA/IPAC IRSA's SIA service, with TAP as the fallback. It downloads only small cutouts, never full frames, using range reads from IRSA's public AWS S3 mirror with IRSA's cutout service as the fallback. Then it subtracts the zodiacal light model and masks bad pixels using each file's FLAGS bits. It reprojects every frame onto one north-up 6.15″/px grid and stacks frames per survey pass over the wavelength channels common to all passes, so a blink compares like with like. Gaia field stars are used to check the alignment and correct it when needed. The browser applies the stretch, blink and difference on a canvas, so the controls respond instantly.

Validation and honesty: Barnard's Star moved 1.643 px against a Gaia prediction of 1.669 px: a 0.041 px vector error, within the 0.2 px limit. epsilon Indi B has a 0.031 px error. WISE 0855 detection and the RW Aur and R Dra variability are reported as not validated. The app makes no discovery claims, and every number shown comes from our code.

Reliability: Real SPHEREx cutouts of the five targets ship with the app, so the presets render even if IRSA or our API is down. The 47 prepared fields are served from a public Azure Blob cache.

Tools and Stack: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy and s3fs; React, Vite and TypeScript. On Azure, one Docker container runs on Azure Container Apps, built by GitHub Actions through Azure Container Registry, with a managed identity instead of stored secrets. Blob Storage holds the render cache, an Azure Functions timer watches for new data, and Application Insights and Log Analytics provide monitoring.

Impact and Creativity: We brought a historic discovery technique to a brand-new all-sky, 102-colour infrared survey and made it a link anyone can open. Citizen scientists, classrooms and astronomers can do a quick look before downloading anything.
